name: Contact Page
summary: One channel, three fields, and a sentence about what happens after you press send. The page that decides whether a stranger believes a human is behind the site.
lede: A contact page is a promise, not a form. The visitor is deciding whether sending a message will produce a reply, and the only evidence available is how much the page is willing to commit to: a response time, a named person, an address that is not a form.
brief: The default generated contact page has a five-field form, no email address, no response time, and a map. It answers none of the questions the visitor has, which are: will anyone read this, how long will it take, and can I reach a person without filling in a form.

The version below makes three commitments a form cannot: a plain email address in text, a stated reply window, and a short list of what is genuinely out of scope. That last one is counter-intuitive but it raises trust, because a page that accepts everything reads as a page nobody reads.

sections.name: One primary channel
sections.why: A plain address in selectable text, or a three-field form. Two competing channels split attention and double the maintenance.

sections.name: What happens next
sections.why: Who reads it, in what time, from which timezone. This single paragraph is the highest-value copy on the page.

sections.name: Scoped reasons to write
sections.why: Four named categories with an example each. They route the message before it is written and reduce the vague ones.

sections.name: What is out of scope
sections.why: Stated plainly: no guest posts, no link exchanges, no support for third-party builds. It filters spam and signals that a human set the policy.

sections.name: Alternatives
sections.why: Where else the answer might already exist: docs, FAQ, status page. It deflects a share of messages before they are sent.

sections.name: Privacy note
sections.why: One sentence on what happens to the message and a link to the policy. Required for any site collecting personal data, and cheap to include.

promptLines: Build a contact page for {{SITE}}.
AUDIENCE

Someone with a specific reason to write — a correction, a licensing question, a broken page — who is deciding whether it is worth the effort. They are not browsing; they arrived from a footer link and will leave in under a minute if the page feels like a funnel.
STRUCTURE (exactly this order)
1. A single sentence stating who reads these messages. Not a form yet.
2. The primary channel: {{CHANNEL}} If an address, it is selectable text in large type with a mailto link, plus the timezone. If a form, it has {{FIELDS}}
3. What happens next: one short paragraph naming the reply window in working days, the timezone, and what to do if no reply arrives.
4. Reasons to write: exactly four, each with one example sentence. Written as a definition list, not as cards.
5. Out of scope: one short list of what is not answered and why. Keep it to three items.
6. Alternatives: two or three links to places that already answer common questions.
7. Privacy note: one sentence about what happens to a submitted message, with a link to the privacy policy.
STYLE
{{STYLE}}
MOTION
{{MOTION}}
COPY RULES
- State a response time in working days, not as soon as possible.
- Name the timezone with its UTC offset.
- Never write fill out the form below to get in touch. Say who reads it.
- Every out-of-scope item is stated without apology and without justification beyond one clause.
- No marketing copy on this page. No newsletter signup, no chat widget.
CONSTRAINTS
- The address or form must be visible without scrolling at 390x844.
- A form has at most three visible fields; anything else is collected in the reply.
- Every field has a visible label, not a placeholder used as a label.
- The success state replaces the form in place and confirms the reply window again.
- No CAPTCHA unless spam is a demonstrated problem; use a honeypot field instead.
OUTPUT
One page. Self-contained. The form works without JavaScript up to the point of submission.

options.label: Reference site
options.value: a reference site that publishes documentation and prompts, run by one person, where most messages are corrections

options.label: Product company
options.value: a product company where messages split between sales, support and partnership, and the page must route people before they write

options.label: Personal site
options.value: a personal site where the owner is the only reader and most messages are about the work itself

options.label: Plain email
options.value: a plain email address set at 1.3rem in body text as a mailto link, with the timezone noted beside it and a total absence of any form
options.hint: The most trustworthy option and the least work to maintain.

options.label: Three-field form
options.value: a three-field form — name, email, message — with a real success state, plus the email address underneath for anyone who would rather not use a form

options.label: Email plus calendar
options.value: the email address plus one scheduling link described as a 20-minute call, not as a demo or a discovery session

options.label: Three
options.value: three fields: name, email, and one message box. No subject line, no topic dropdown.
options.hint: Fewest fields that still identify a person.

options.label: Four with topic
options.value: four fields: name, email, a topic select with three options that determines who receives it, and a message box.
options.hint: Only worth it when messages genuinely route to different people.

options.label: Editorial
options.value: Editorial: warm off-white page, serif headings, the address set large in the serif face, a 62-character measure for prose, hairlines instead of cards.

options.label: Product neutral
options.value: Product neutral: white page, 1px bordered inputs at 44px, one accent on the submit button, section labels at 0.72rem uppercase, generous spacing between the four sections.

options.label: Swiss
options.value: Swiss: white page, strict twelve-column grid, the address aligned to column one at 2rem in Helvetica, one red rule under the page title, no rounded corners anywhere.

options.label: None
options.value: No animation beyond the form's own state transitions. Nobody wants to watch a contact page perform.

options.label: Success only
options.value: One 200ms fade on the success message replacing the form. Nothing else animates.

change.note: Email beats a form for trust and loses nothing except spam protection. A form is justified when messages need routing, not when the site owner simply prefers one.
A topic dropdown is only honest if the options lead to genuinely different inboxes. If everything lands in one place, the field is decoration and slows the sender down.

This changes the out-of-scope list, which is the part most worth writing carefully. A reference site says no to guest posts; a product company says no to feature requests that belong in the issue tracker.
Swap the block whole. On this page the address is the visual anchor: set it large in whatever typeface the style uses, and keep everything else quiet.
None. This is the page where a spinner before a confirmation costs more trust than it saves milliseconds.

builders.name: v0
builders.note: Ask for the copy first, then the layout. The text on this page is the product, and generating the layout first tends to produce a form where a paragraph was needed.

builders.name: Lovable
builders.note: It will add a map and a chat widget. Both are noise on a page whose job is to state one address and one response time.

builders.name: Bolt
builders.note: Ask for the form to post to a real endpoint you name, or to a mailto fallback. A form with no action attribute is the most common defect on generated contact pages.

builders.name: Cursor / Claude Code
builders.note: Keep the four reasons-to-write and the out-of-scope list in the markup rather than a CMS, so the page stays readable with JavaScript disabled.

failures.title: A form with no address
failures.body: Visitors who distrust forms — privacy-conscious, corporate, or simply burned before — have nowhere to go. Publishing the address costs nothing and keeps the option open.

failures.title: No response promise
failures.body: A page that says we will get back to you has said nothing. Within two working days is a commitment, and it is the single line most likely to convert a hesitant sender.

failures.title: Accepting everything
failures.body: A page that welcomes all enquiries equally signals that nobody reads them. Naming what is out of scope is what makes the rest credible.

failures.title: Placeholder used as a label
failures.body: Text that disappears the moment someone types means the field's meaning disappears with it. Labels above inputs, always visible, on every field.
